For small initial semimajor axes (black), the inclination distribution is isotropic because (i) nearly all orbits become EMRIs and (ii) the initial conditions are isotropic. As the initial semimajor axis increases, the EMRI inclination distribution becomes more prograde (red). For comparison, fixed-inclination models are shown: an isotropic case (less prograde than the diffusive results) and a  Gaussian case (remaining strongly prograde/retrograde). This demonstrates that inclination diffusion efficiently washes out initial conditions at large semimajor axes.

2610.18964.abstract: Extreme mass ratio inspirals (EMRIs) are expected to be a major source of gravitational waves (GWs) for the future {\it Laser Interferometer Space Antenna} ({\it LISA}). An EMRI occurs when a compact object, driven by the emission of gravitational radiation, slowly inspirals into a massive black hole (MBH). The classical formation channel involves repeated two-body interactions within dense nuclear star clusters. However, both EMRI event rates and the expected distribution of their orbital parameters remain highly uncertain. A major source of this uncertainty is the poorly constrained ratio between gradually inspiraling EMRIs and direct plunges, which do not produce detectable GWs. While most studies of astrophysical EMRI production focus on the Schwarzschild limit, previous work examining the Kerr metric found that the spin of the central MBH can significantly affect the EMRI-to-plunge ratio. This enhancement depends sensitively on orbital inclination, yet earlier studies held inclination fixed. In this work, we develop the mathematical framework describing inclination evolution driven by two-body encounters evolving along Kerr geodesics. By implementing 3D diffusion into Monte Carlo simulations, we show that initially prograde orbits may evolve into retrograde states, thereby converting potential EMRIs into plunges or vice versa. We estimate the EMRI-to-plunge ratio and find that substantial MBH spin enhances the EMRI rate by a factor of $\sim 2.5$. Additionally, even for a non-spinning MBH, modeling the orbits as relativistic geodesics rather than Newtonian trajectories increases the number of EMRIs by a similar factor of $\sim 2.5$. The distribution of Kerr EMRI inclinations has a substantial prograde bias that may aid in identifying the subset of loss cone EMRIs within large future EMRI samples.

2610.18968.abstract: The Little Red Dots (LRDs) are compact, red sources, abundant at $4 \lesssim z \lesssim 9$ and likely powered by massive black holes. Photometric studies have found blue companions around them, but none has yet been confirmed spectroscopically. This Letter presents the only two LRD-companion pairs with spectroscopy of both members in the literature: "Waltz" at $z = 3.9$ and "Tango" at $z = 5.5$, with projected separations of $3.6$ and $2.5$ kpc. Both companions lie at the redshift of their LRD, within $132 \, \rm km \, s^{-1}$ and $57 \, \rm km \, s^{-1}$, and are physically identical, but $524$ Myr apart: starbursts $\lesssim 50$ Myr old, metal-poor ($0.2 \, \rm Z_\odot$), dust-free, dynamically cold, and as bright as the LRDs themselves in the rest-frame UV. The LRD in Waltz hosts a $\approx 3 \times 10^{6} \, \rm M_\odot$ black hole accreting at half the Eddington rate, a factor of a few above the birth mass of a direct collapse black hole, and is embedded in gas as metal-poor as its companion. Orbital modeling shows that Tango is bound in $81\%$ of the allowed orbits and that Waltz is bound if its host halo exceeds $5 \times 10^{10} \, \rm M_\odot$. Both blue companions then merge with their respective LRD within a few hundred Myr. We conclude that we are observing what heavy seeding requires: a young black hole beside the metal-poor starburst that the synchronized-pair scenario predicts, in the last steps of a cosmic dance that ends in a merger, and in a galaxy seeded by its black hole.

2610.18969.abstract: Wave cold dark matter (wave CDM) is a well-motivated variant within the collisionless CDM paradigm, in which the de~Broglie wavelengths of ultralight bosons become relevant on galactic scales. While many of the previous tests of wave CDM have focused on small-scale tensions involving solitonic cores and certain soliton--halo relations in galaxies, the radial acceleration relation (RAR) provides a complementary test: for a given baryonic mass distribution, it probes whether the DM halo can reproduce the observed total gravitational field. In this work we test wave CDM against the RAR using eight X-ray elliptical galaxies from the compilation of Lelli et al. We perform a suite of 3D Schrödinger--Poisson simulations and evolve the wave-CDM halos to virialized quasi-stationary states. For each galaxy and each adopted boson mass, we select the realization whose final snapshot most closely matches the empirical RAR. We find that the selected wave-CDM realizations for these elliptical galaxies can reproduce the RAR without including baryonic feedback or dark-matter self-interactions. At the boson mass $m_a=10^{-23}$eV, the combined fit to the eight galaxies gives $a_0=1.19\times10^{-10}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, consistent with the canonical value inferred from disk galaxies. When the boson mass is varied over $3\times 10^{-24}$ eV $\le m_a \le 2\times 10^{-23}$ eV, the best-fit value of $a_0$ changes by only $\sim 11\%$, and this variation shows no systematic trend with $m_a$. This insensitivity to boson mass arises because, over the radial range relevant for the RAR, the virialized halos are supported mainly by their velocity field, whereas the boson-mass-dependent quantum-pressure term is dynamically subdominant. These results show that wave CDM can reproduce the RAR in elliptical galaxies, and provide a new galactic-scale test of the model beyond the previous focus on solitonic cores.

2610.18978.abstract: Action-based distribution functions $f(\mathbf{J})$ provide a powerful description of stellar systems. Consequently, the construction of physically accurate and dynamically stable $f(\mathbf{J})$ for galactic components has emerged as a key challenge in the field. In this study, we present GroArnold, a computational framework designed to construct analytical $f(\mathbf{J})$ expressions for axisymmetric and triaxial galaxies and dark matter halos. The framework integrates modules for $N$-body initial condition generation, $N$-body simulation, angle--action variable estimation, and distribution-function fitting into a unified workflow. It supports a wide range of density profiles and kinematic properties, and is uniquely designed to generate stable $N$-body models for user-specified galactic systems, with the aim of obtaining an $f(\mathbf{J})$ that approximates a dynamically stable and physically consistent state. To this end, we extend the triaxial Stäckel Fudge method of the TACT code, implemented in our Nbody-TACT module, to enable action estimation directly from $N$-body gravitational potentials. GroArnold provides a robust and flexible tool for deriving numerically empirical, explicitly analytical distribution functions for user-specified galaxies or halos, thereby facilitating a wide range of practical $f(\mathbf{J})$-based modeling applications. In addition, it serves as a powerful tool for investigating the dynamics of realistic triaxial galaxies and halos beyond the scope of traditional spherical or axisymmetric models. We assessed the accuracy of the output $f(\mathbf{J})$ by comparing its predicted spatial and velocity distributions with those of the input $N$-body snapshot, and confirmed that it provides a reasonably accurate representation of the input. The code is modular, publicly available, and designed to support future extensions and adaptations.

2610.18979.abstract: Charged dust in magnetized gas is subject to aerodynamic drag and the Lorentz force, both of which can be difficult to model numerically in a fluid simulation where their characteristic timescales are shorter than the timestep set by the Courant condition. We present a two-stage general implicit Runge-Kutta (GIRK) source integrator for multifluid charged dust coupled to an ideal magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) gas, implemented in the open source GPU-accelerated quokka code. Drag and Lorentz forces are advanced together in one implicit source update, avoiding errors in the terminal drift that can arise when the two forces are advanced in separate substeps. The timestep is compared with a drag-Lorentz timescale to select between resolved and stiff branches. The resolved branch uses Gauss-Legendre coefficients, while the stiff branch uses a coefficient set designed to recover the terminal drift set by the drag-Lorentz balance. We also allow the dust stopping time and charge-to-mass ratio to depend on the evolving state, evaluating them separately at the two implicit stage states and solving the resulting nonlinear stage equations by Picard iteration. The source update conserves total gas-dust momentum, and its computational cost scales linearly with the number of dust species. Tests reproduce the expected drag damping and terminal drift, confirm the predicted gyromotion amplitude and phase errors, demonstrate accurate treatment of state-dependent source coefficients, and recover the expected wave, shock, and instability dynamics in dusty MHD flows.

2610.18985.abstract: Two-body collisional relaxation in stellar systems is conventionally estimated using the classical Chandrasekhar theory, in which a subject star is assumed to be embedded in a homogeneous medium of field stars and their velocity distribution taken to be isotropic and Gaussian. Real stellar systems, however, can exhibit pronounced spatial and kinematic substructures. We investigate how such substructures -- particularly the non-classical spatial inhomogeneity -- modify the two-body diffusion coefficient. We retain hyperbolic two-body encounters but generalize the encounter calculation by integrating explicitly over the spatial distribution $n(\mathbf{r})$, while evaluating the velocity contribution from the full distribution $f_v(\mathbf{v})$. This yields a separable tensor expression for the diffusion coefficient. We find that spatial substructure produces the dominant enhancement. The enhancement of the diffusion coefficient increases systematically as the effective fractal dimension $D_{\rm frac}$ decreases, $\log \zeta_r(D_\text{frac}) \sim \left(1-D_\text{frac}/3\right)^q$ with $q \approx 4.28$. For the observationally motivated case with $D_{\rm frac}\approx 1.5$, the enhancement is moderate, whereas substantially lower fractal dimensions produce much larger enhancements. In contrast, the anisotropic, power-law-tailed, and fractal-like velocity distributions modify the diffusion coefficient only by factors of order unity. Our representative substructured model yields enhancement ratios $\zeta_r\simeq3.45$ and $\zeta_v\simeq1.33$ when the measured particle-number trends are extrapolated to $N=10^{11}$, corresponding to an overall enhancement of $\zeta\simeq4.6$. Therefore, within the two-body encounter framework and the commonly used separable distribution functions, the enhanced collisional relaxation still has little impact on the mean-field nature of typical galactic systems.

2610.18998.abstract: We report the detection of the convective-transition gap along the lower main sequence (MS) of the Galactic globular cluster (GC) 47 Tucanae using deep James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations. We analyse the stellar luminosity function (LF) in the vicinity of the gap location using two independent colour-magnitude diagrams (CMDs). In both cases, the LF is characterised by a narrow gap followed by a discontinuous increase in the stellar number counts, and presents an overall morphology qualitatively consistent with that reported in previous studies. By modelling the observed LFs with an empirical likelihood model, we estimate the statistical significance of the observed feature. Additional JWST passbands exhibit similar signatures, providing further evidence for the presence of a discontinuity.

2610.19030.abstract: Understanding how galaxies populate and grow within dark matter haloes is essential for linking the observed evolution of galaxies to the hierarchical growth of structure. We present a galaxy clustering analysis using optical and near-infrared data from the UltraVISTA and VIDEO surveys covering $9.3$ deg$^2$ across the COSMOS, XMM-LSS and ECDF-S fields, $\sim 5\times$ larger than previous comparable studies, providing sufficient volume to determine the halo occupation of the most massive galaxies to $z\sim 4$. We measure the angular two-point correlation function for stellar-mass-selected galaxies over $0.25<z<4$ and by combining the three fields, we reduce the cosmic variance by a factor of $\sim2$ compared to the individual fields. The stellar-to-halo mass ratio peaks at a halo mass of $M_{h}\approx10^{12} {\rm M}_{\odot}$ and is a maximum at $z\sim 1$. For the most massive galaxies, the peak halo mass ($M_{h}^{\rm peak}$) increases from $z=1\rightarrow 0$, while the peak stellar mass in such haloes remains approximately constant, indicating that at $z<1$ massive galaxy formation becomes less efficient. We also find a steady increase in the satellite fraction since $z\sim 1$, from which we infer that massive halos continue to grow hierarchically while their central galaxies experience suppressed stellar-mass growth. We suggest this is due to the central massive galaxies having their growth controlled by feedback from active galactic nuclei feedback, likely from low-power stochastic radio emission.

2610.19079.abstract: The MeerKAT Observations of the Saraswati Supercluster (MOSS) is an ongoing project attempting to study the radio and optical properties of the core region of the Saraswati supercluster (z = 0.28) and will eventually entail a full survey of the entire supercluster region. Here we use radio catalogs from previous deep pilot MeerKAT L-band (1.28 GHz) observations (angular resolution of 8 arcsec) of the core region of the Saraswati supercluster. The region hosts two galaxy clusters representing distinct environments: The most massive cluster Abell 2631, and the second most massive cluster ZwCl2341, that is significantly more dynamically active. The deep radio catalogs of these clusters were combined with spectroscopic redshifts (mainly from DESI DR1 and SDSS DR16) and optical photometry catalogs of the cluster member galaxy source population. We use these redshifts together with the 1.4GHz MeerKAT flux densities to derive the dust-free star-formation rate (SFR) and evaluate various trends in the radio SFG and AGN galaxy populations. We find that the actively merging cluster ZwCL2341 has an increased star-forming galaxy population compared to A2631 with up to 4 times more star-forming galaxies. When looking at SFG-related radio processes we see s enhanced SF-related activity in ZwCL2341 with SF-related radio processes dominates entirely over AGN-related radio processes. This suggests that dynamically active environments associated with cluster assembly, such as mergers, have enhanced SF radio-activity and increased SFG (both radio and non-radio) galaxy population compared to lesser active systems.

2610.19126.abstract: We analyzed a sample of 494 galaxies from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) I-IV that have unusual properties. They display broadened Mg II $\lambda$2798 line emission, as would be expected of Type 1 active galactic nuclei (AGN). However, they have weak or absent broad Balmer lines though broadened Balmer lines often accompany broadened ultraviolet lines in Type 1 AGN spectra. We performed a spectral decomposition of these "broad Mg II galaxies'' to assess whether they can be considered fading AGN. The Balmer lines are more responsive to changes in the AGN continuum than the Mg II line. As the AGN power source fades, broad H$\beta$ and then H$\alpha$ will weaken and eventually disappear, leaving broad Mg II as a signpost of a more active past. In support of this interpretation, we found that broad Mg II galaxies have weaker AGN luminosities and lower accretion rates (parameterized by the Eddington ratio) than typical Type 1 quasars from SDSS. The Eddington ratio of broad Mg II galaxies are similar to dim-state changing-look AGN, with an average value $\lesssim$1\%, which is the threshold at which the inner region of a geometrically thin accretion disk is thought to evaporate and be replaced by a geometrically thick radiatively inefficient accretion flow in stellar-mass black holes. Broad Mg II galaxies may represent the penultimate stage in a changing-look AGN sequence prior to the complete disappearance of all broad lines.

2610.19146.abstract: The processes that rapidly quench massive galaxies and maintain their quiescence remain poorly understood. Substantial molecular gas reservoirs can survive this shutdown in post-starburst galaxies, raising the question of what prevents the remaining gas from efficiently forming stars. We present deep, subarcsecond VLA 6 GHz observations of 52 massive SQuIGGLE post-starburst galaxies at $z\sim0.7$ to test the prevalence and mechanical impact of radio activity during the gas-rich post-burst phase. We detect 6 GHz continuum emission in 18/52 galaxies ($\approx$35\%), spanning $\log(L_{1.4\,{\rm GHz}}/{\rm W\,Hz^{-1}})\simeq23.0$--$25.0$ and generally exceeding the contributions expected from ongoing star formation and the fading starburst, favoring an AGN origin. Ancillary data at other wavelengths provide little evidence for a population of luminous, radiatively efficient AGN, suggesting that these sources are instead dominated by comparatively weak, mechanically powered radio AGN. Radio activity is strongly concentrated within the first $\sim$200 Myr post-burst and is predominantly associated with galaxies retaining substantial gas reservoirs. Above a common radio luminosity threshold, the radio detection fraction is enhanced by a factor of $\approx$2.5 relative to the radio AGN candidate fraction in mass- and redshift-matched quiescent LEGA-C galaxies, primarily due to lower power sources. For efficient jet--ISM coupling, the inferred mechanical power could supply the approximate energy required to unbind the molecular gas on timescales comparable to its observed decline. Together, these results identify a population of radiatively inefficient AGN hosted predominantly by young, gas-rich post-starburst galaxies at $z\sim0.7$ and suggest that they may have a role in maintaining inefficient star formation.

2610.19163.abstract: Obtaining accurate estimates of the gas column density $\mathrm{N(H_2)}$ is crucial to determine the physical conditions of the molecular gas in the Interstellar Medium. This paper introduces the "Multi-Tracer Column Density Synthesis" (MT-CDS) technique, a new empirical approach to derive high dynamic-range column density maps with interferometers such as ALMA. We have compared the integrated intensity maps of two density selective tracers, namely HNC (1-0) and $\mathrm{N_2H^+}$ (1-0), obtained with IRAM-30m with ancillary Herschel column density estimates in seven star-forming regions in Orion and derived individual temperature-corrected conversion factors for each of these tracers. We applied these conversion factors obtained at low-resolution into similar high sensitivity ALMA observations to derive independent column density maps describing both the low $N_\mathrm{HNC}\mathrm{(H_2)}$ and high $N_\mathrm{N_2H^+}\mathrm{(H_2)}$ column density components at high spatial resolution (4.5"). We also combined these independent maps into estimates for the total gas column density gas $N_\mathrm{tot}\mathrm{(H_2)}$ sampling more than two orders of magnitude in column density between $\sim 10^{21.5}-10^{23.5}$ cm$^{-2}$. A comparison with independent ArTeMiS column density maps at intermediate resolution (8") shows typical deviations of $\lesssim$0.2 dex from our MT-CDS gas column density estimates. We obtained individual column density maps in five of our targets at $\sim$2000 au resolution in which ALMA observations were available, that is a factor of $\sim$5 better than originally calibrated. These results demonstrate the potential of this MT-CDS technique to retrieve accurate, high dynamic range $N\mathrm{(H_2)}$ total gas column density estimates at interferometric resolution combining multiple molecular line tracers.

2610.19182.title: Galactic Outflows and Star-Formation Quenching: A JWST Perspective

figures.caption: Figure 1: Strengths and weaknesses of outflow tracers commonly used at cosmic noon (top). The differences between emission line and absorption line tracers are illustrated using zoom-ins of an example $z\sim$ 2 galaxy spectrum (bottom; Davies et al., in prep). Broad optical emission line components tracing ionized outflows are detected in many galaxies at cosmic noon, but they do not trace the dominant outflow phase and often are not sensitive to outflows in low mass galaxies because they blend with the much stronger ISM emission. UV absorption lines require a bright rest-frame UV continuum and generally cannot be used to probe outflows from dusty or quenching galaxies. 2610.19182.abstract: Outflows driven by active galactic nuclei (AGN) are widely considered a key mechanism for regulating and quenching star formation in massive galaxies. However, direct observational evidence linking outflows to quenching has remained elusive for decades. This article reviews recent findings for massive galaxies at cosmic noon ($z\sim 2$), based on sensitive James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations tracing both star formation histories (through Balmer absorption lines) and neutral outflows (through blueshifted NaID absorption). Neutral outflows are found in $\sim$ 25 - 50% of massive ($\log(M_*/M_\odot)>$ 10) galaxies, independent of star formation rate. Outflows from star-forming galaxies are consistent with being powered by star-formation and/or AGN activity, whereas outflows from quiescent systems are generally attributed to current or previous AGN activity. There is growing evidence that recent rapid quenching of star-formation is associated with powerful AGN-driven outflows with mass loading factors $\eta \gtrsim$ 1 - 10. The neutral gas dominates the outflow mass budget but in most cases its velocity is below the halo escape velocity, indicating that this gas may form part of a galactic fountain. Detections of neutral gas inflows and residual cold gas reservoirs in quiescent galaxies suggest that other feedback mechanisms such as AGN heating are required to keep galaxies quenched over long timescales. We highlight the potential of multiphase outflow measurements to constrain feedback models, describe the main systematic uncertainties in mass outflow rate measurements, and discuss how the $z\sim 2$ results inform our understanding of the formation of the earliest massive quiescent galaxies.

2610.19312.abstract: We study the relative contributions of mergers and accretion to the assembly of dark matter haloes within the framework of Excursion Set Theory (EST). We extend a variance-discretized merger-tree algorithm, which recursively reconstructs all branches of a complete merger tree and introduces a merger-ratio criterion for distinguishing mergers from accretion. The method is validated by comparing the resulting progenitor distributions with the analytical conditional first up-crossing distribution, showing excellent agreement over a wide range of halo masses and redshifts. We find that the accretion contribution depends strongly on the adopted merger-ratio threshold. For large merger ratios ($MR=0.1$--$0.25$), accretion accounts for up to $\sim70\%$ of the mass growth of massive haloes, whereas including all resolved mergers ($MR=10^{-6}$) reduces the accretion contribution to $\sim40\%$. These values are in good agreement with previous N-body simulation results. The accreted mass exhibits a nearly self-similar distribution in the mass-redshift plane, with the dominant contribution arising from progenitors in the range $10^{-3}M_0 \lesssim M \lesssim 10^{-1}M_0$ and predominantly at $0.5 \lesssim z \lesssim 2$. Our results demonstrate that EST-based merger trees provide an accurate and computationally efficient framework for investigating halo assembly and quantifying the relative roles of mergers and accretion in hierarchical structure formation.

2610.19317.abstract: Whether dense environments accelerate SMBH growth during cosmic reionization remains uncertain because X-ray constraints on $z>6$ protoclusters are rare. We analyze $\sim865$ ks of Chandra observations of J0910-0414 quasar field, a massive protocluster at $z=6.63$. We construct a catalog of 251 X-ray sources and search for AGN among 21 spectroscopically confirmed members, excluding the central quasar. This is the first systematic X-ray AGN census in a $z>6$ protocluster; none of the members is individually detected. Stacking all members ($\sim17$ Ms total exposure) yields no significant signal and limits the average rest-frame 2-10 keV luminosity to $\langle L_{\rm 2-10~keV}\rangle\leq9.54\times10^{42}~\rm erg~s^{-1}$. The null result gives a central 90% Jeffreys upper bound of $f_{\rm AGN}<0.09$. After accounting for the spatially varying sensitivity, the field Compton-thin X-ray luminosity function predicts $N_{\rm exp,field}=0.0356$ AGN in the surveyed volume. Assuming the overdensity profile of AGNs in this protocluster is the same as that of galaxies determined by Wang et al. (2024), the expected AGN count becomes $N_{\rm exp}=0.131$. Zero detections then imply a one-sided 90% upper limit of $\eta_{\rm rel}<17.5$ on any additional X-ray AGN enhancement beyond that associated with the galaxy overdensity. Although $\eta_{\rm rel}<17.5$ permits more than an order-of-magnitude enhancement, the data show no significant excess of X-ray-detectable AGN in J0910-0414 protocluster. The present X-ray data may miss heavily obscured, intrinsically X-ray-weak, or intermittently accreting SMBHs; the non-detection therefore does not rule out AGNs among the member galaxies.

2610.19318.abstract: We combine wide-area COSMOS-3D observations with deeper GOODS-N data from JWST/NIRCam F444W wide-field slitless spectroscopy to trace cosmic star formation over $z\sim0$--9. The observations cover approximately $0.33~\mathrm{deg}^2$ in COSMOS and $60.9~\mathrm{arcmin}^2$ in GOODS-N, with typical $3\sigma$ integrated line-flux limits of $3.2\times10^{-18}$ and $1.04\times10^{-18}~\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}\,cm^{-2}}$, respectively. The common $3.9$--$5.0\,\mu$m wavelength window probes Br$\alpha$, Br$\beta$, Pa$\alpha$, Pa$\beta$, H$\alpha$, and H$\beta$ across the local Universe, cosmic noon, and reionization. Our final sample contains 9146 galaxies, including 7883 in COSMOS and 1263 in GOODS-N. COSMOS constrains luminous emitters, while GOODS-N extends the luminosity functions toward fainter sources. We measure dust-corrected line luminosities, account for line-detection completeness, and convert the six lines to equivalent H$\alpha$ luminosities assuming Case B recombination. Schechter fits reveal an increase in the characteristic H$\alpha$-equivalent luminosity toward cosmic noon. Integrating the resulting star formation rate functions above $0.24\,M_\odot\,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, we trace the cosmic star formation rate density from the local Universe to reionization. The combined Brackett, Paschen, and Balmer measurements are broadly consistent with the canonical UV- and IR-based cosmic star formation history at $z\lesssim6$. Fixed-slope tests show that the H$\beta$ estimate at $z\sim8$ remains sensitive to the external photometric faint-end constraint and extrapolation below our spectroscopic limit. These measurements provide complementary constraints on the distribution and integrated rate of star formation across cosmic time.

2610.19319.abstract: Molecular hydrogen (H$_2$) is the fundamental component of the molecular gas reservoir that fuels star formation and black hole growth. While prominent hot H$_2$ emission ($\gtrsim 1000$ K) has been explored in nearby galaxies, its excitation mechanisms at higher redshifts remain poorly constrained. We present a systematic study of hot molecular gas traced via ro-vibrational H$_2$ emitters at z~0.2-1.5 using JWST slitless spectroscopy. Exploiting JWST's great sensitivity to near-infrared H$_2$ ro-vibrational transitions such as H$_2$ 1-0 S(1), we build a sample of 144 H$_2$-luminous galaxies and characterize their multi-wavelength properties. About 96.5% and 80% of these galaxies are detected in the radio and far-infrared (FIR) bands, respectively, and their hot H$_2$ emission strongly correlates with the radio and FIR radiation. Based on radio excess, X-ray emission, and optical diagnostics, 62 sources (43%) exhibit significant AGN activity. The H$_2$ line luminosities of the sample show a sublinear dependence on radio luminosity, while the relation between the H$_2$ luminosities and total infrared luminosities is approximately linear after excluding the radio-excess sources. These scaling relations suggest that star formation provides a baseline contribution to hot H$_2$ excitation, while radio-excess sources require an additional contribution from AGN-related processes such as jet- or wind-driven shocks. These results reveal a multi-channel excitation scenario and shed new light on the interplay between star formation, AGN activity, and the interstellar medium during galaxy evolution.

2610.19320.abstract: The role of the large-scale environment in regulating AGN activity remains an open question. We investigate the Mpc-scale environments of 70 AGNs at $z=1.1$-$1.5$ using a highly complete sample of 3,419 Pa$\alpha$ emitters with accurate spectroscopic redshifts from JWST slitless spectroscopic survey. This dataset allows us to robustly trace the environments and quantify the environmental dependence of AGN properties. We measure the eighth-nearest-neighbor surface density of Pa$\alpha$ emitters around each AGN, probing $\sim$1.5 pMpc scale environments. We find that this environmental density exhibits a weak positive correlation with radio luminosity. Radio-bright AGNs tend to reside in statistically denser environments than their radio-faint counterparts. The environmental density also has a positive correlation with the Eddington ratio and a weak negative correlation with the central black hole mass, implying more efficient black hole accretion in dense environments. We construct Pa$\alpha$ luminosity functions (LFs) in AGN environments and find that they are systematically elevated relative to the field Pa$\alpha$ LF. In addition, their faint-end slopes are shallower, suggesting accelerated galaxy growth and enhanced quenching of star formation. As Pa$\alpha$ emitters trace gas-rich, star-forming galaxies, our results support a scenario in which the large-scale cold gas promotes AGN activity at cosmic noon.

2610.19379.abstract: Correctly modeling the dust attenuation law in galaxies is essential to properly inferring their growth and physical properties. With the rapid discovery of $z>6$ galaxies by JWST and lack of constraints on the properties of dust at these redshifts, we must turn to theoretical models to predict the properties of dust at these redshifts. In this paper, we develop a theoretical foundation for the nature of high-redshift attenuation laws. We analyze $107$ cosmological zoom-in simulations of galaxies run with the SMUGGLE galaxy formation model. SMUGGLE includes an explicitly modeled multiphase interstellar medium and a state-of-the-art dust model with a self-consistently evolving dust grain size distribution. We forward model these simulations with the radiative transfer package POWDERDAY to produce synthetic spectra and attenuation curves for a set of $z=5-15$, $M_*\sim10^{6.5}-10^{10}\; \mathrm{M}_{\odot}$ galaxies. We find evidence for flatter attenuation curves than the commonly used locally-calibrated literature attenuation laws assumed when modeling high-redshift galaxies. The vast majority of our attenuation curves also lack the 2175 Angstrom absorption feature. Our attenuation laws do not evolve strongly over $z=15-5$, which we attribute to relatively constant fractions of small grains up to $z=4$ in our simulations. We present a set of simulation-informed priors on dust attenuation law parameterization that could be implemented in SED fitting codes. There is an anti-correlation between galaxy mass and attenuation curve slope and positive correlation between galaxy mass and $A_V$, which we attribute to dust growth becoming efficient in our massive galaxies with $\log{M_*/\mathrm{M}_{\odot}}\gtrsim9$ and with ISM conditions above a critical metallicity threshold.

2610.19567.abstract: We present self-consistent $N$-body/hydrodynamical simulations of isolated, Milky Way-like galaxies with stellar and gaseous disks. By varying the initial gas fraction, we find that gas delays bar formation and, in the most gas-rich model, suppresses it by exciting higher-order spiral modes and promoting early central mass growth. Once a bar forms, continued gas inflow and gravitational torques weaken the bar and inhibit its secular slowdown, keeping bars in the gas-bearing models shorter and predominantly in the fast-bar regime, while the gas-free bar evolves into the slow-bar regime. Stars and gas respond differently to the same barred potential. While the mean stellar velocity field is well described by a smooth bisymmetric pattern, the cold and warm gas follow elongated, $x_1$-like streamlines with sharp shock-induced velocity transitions, producing sawtooth-like radial and archlike tangential velocity profiles. Despite these strong noncircular motions, their azimuthally averaged tangential velocities closely follow the circular velocity over most of the disk. By contrast, the hot gas is dominated by stellar feedback and thermal pressure and is largely decoupled from the ordered bar-driven flow. To describe these bar-driven gas flows, we introduce the barflow model, a phenomenological description of non-sinusoidal gas streaming motions with a radially varying shock-front phase. Mock line-of-sight velocity-fitting experiments show that the barflow model recovers the intrinsic rotation curve, bar-driven velocity perturbations, and radial gas transport more accurately than the conventional bisymmetric model.

2610.19703.abstract: Gravitational microlensing probes unresolved quasar accretion disc structure and compact objects in lens galaxies and is an important systematic in strong-lens time-delay cosmography. Most analyses use static microlensing map simulations because evolving individual microlenses and caustics is computationally prohibitive. We present Microcaustics, a GPU-accelerated Python package built on PyTorch for dynamical microlensing of time-dependent extended sources in strong gravitational lenses. It combines a local-exact/far-field deflection solver, source-directed lens-plane scouting with temporal reuse, and biquadratic inverse polygon mapping (IPM). GPU batching and fused Triton rasterization accelerate the calculation, while binary caustic labels track source-centred crossings. Across three simulated quadruply lensed quasar systems, our package generates a 10-year, 147-frame multiband light curve in an amortized median of 0.68 s (0.88 s with labels) on a consumer GPU with a median light-curve RMSE of 0.35 mmag, while recovering every reference source-centred caustic crossing. At comparable map accuracy, the batched throughput is 780 times higher than that of a recent CUDA IPM implementation and extrapolates to a speedup of millions relative to classic GPU-D. We demonstrate that our IPM converges as $N_{\rm ray}^{-0.84}$, approaching the idealized $N_{\rm ray}^{-1}$ convergence rate of piecewise-affine IPM and improving upon the $N_{\rm ray}^{-1/2}$ inverse ray-shooting rate. We also introduce a GPU-resident general relativistic and reverberating quasar source model and demonstrate our method with an evolving supernova source. These advances make fully dynamical stellar fields practical for Bayesian and simulation-based inference.

2610.19771.abstract: Dust grains produced in the supernova (SN) ejecta at early ages are partially destroyed in hot gas of the SN remnant. Large grains owing to their inertia can overtake the forward shock front of the remnant and move through the ambient interstellar medium. Using one-dimensional gas dynamics including the dust destruction we study the transport of dust grains inside the SN remnant and the ambient medium. Here we estimate the surviving and escaping mass fractions depending on the cut-off (maximum) size in a power-law distribution of grain sizes. We found that these fractions follow closely each other at late age of the SN remnant, i.e. almost all grains, which have survived in the remnant, leave it for the ambient interstellar medium. At the age of 30 kyr -- the onset of the radiative phase with density $n\sim 1$ cm$^{-3}$ with solar metallicity -- the escaping/surviving mass fractions for the cut-off size of several microns reach about $0.7-0.8$. The major part of these grains have size larger than $1~\mu$m and initially located at distances $\gtrsim 0.2$ of the ejecta core radius. Later dust grains at velocity of several hundreds km/s escaping the remnant continue to be destroyed due to kinetic sputtering in the interstellar medium. Grains with sizes of several microns are destroyed marginally and therefore will survive in the interstellar gas. After decelerating of grains in the medium the surviving mass fraction of grains produced in the SN remnant, which evolves in an ambient gas with $n$ from 1 to 100 cm$^{-3}$, is from $\sim 0.5$ to $\sim 0.3$, respectively, for the cut-off grain size $a_{cut} = 10~\mu$m. A decrease of the cut-off size in the distribution results in lower surviving mass fraction.

2610.19835.abstract: Euclid data is going to lead to the discovery of approximately 10^5 new strong gravitational lenses, thereby increasing the number of known lenses by a factor of 30. Such an impressive jump has the potential to revolutionise the field of strong lensing, by covering an ever-increasing range in the parameter space occupied by the lenses and lensed sources, and by uncovering rare and precious strong lens systems. The first quick data release of Euclid has already revealed hundreds of lenses, giving us a taste of what the final Euclid strong lens sample might look like. These lenses include a variety of objects acting as deflectors, from isolated galaxies to clusters, from early-type galaxies to edge-on disks. As many as four double-source plane lenses, in which one foreground object lenses two galaxies at two different redshifts, have already been discovered. As more data are acquired, it might become possible to detect the strong lensing signature of dwarf galaxy satellites, and to find lenses with an unusually large number of images. In this paper, we try to anticipate the kind of discoveries that these data will bring along.

2610.19838.abstract: The aim of this study is to explore methods for how to identify new quasars with different properties with regard to reddening, redshift, the presence of broad absorption lines from outflows, or other rare properties affecting the broad-band colours. We use Gaia-based astrometric pre-selection to study only sources that have zero parallax and zero proper motion within errors. We subsequently match these sources with information from wide-area photometric surveys and build colour-colour diagrams. Based on these diagrams we select targets for follow-up spectroscopy. In the subsequent analysis we also apply observations from SPHEREx to firmly establish redshifts. We secure spectroscopic observations for 24 sources. Of these, three are found to be stars and the remaining 21 are classified as quasars spanning a redshift range from z=0.139 to z=3.732. The majority of the sources located away from the normal quasar locus in colour-colour diagrams are found to be broad-absorption-line quasars. A single source, the lowest redshift source at z=0.139, is reminiscent of the so-called Little Red Dots found at high redshifts with JWST. Using the simple procedure followed here it is possible to locate previously undiscovered quasars with interesting properties, in particular Broad Absorption Line quasars and quasars with unusual extinction.

2610.19881.abstract: The aromatic infrared bands (AIBs) are observed in a wide variety of astrophysical sources, and now in unprecedented detail by the James Webb space telescope (JWST). These bands are generally attributed to the emission from polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAHs). Our aim is to extract mid-infrared AIB template spectra from JWST observations of the Orion Bar photo-dissociation region that can be used to derive PAH properties from observations of other objects. We used the JWST MIRI-MRS observations from the PDRs4All program. We first isolated the AIBs from the data using a multi-component fitting approach. We then applied a non-negative matrix factorization to the isolated AIB spectra and extracted two templates, named AIBirrad and AIBshield following previous work. The spatial distribution and spectral characteristics of these two spectra suggest that they originate from two chemical distinct populations. We interpret AIBirrad as emission originating from a PAH population strongly exposed to ultra-violet (UV) radiation and mainly composed of large, compact ionized PAHs. Conversely, AIBshield is interpreted as originating from a more shielded population of PAHs, which is less exposed to the UV by being more embedded in the cloud. This population consists of small, asymmetric and mainly neutral PAHs with bonded aliphatic side groups. These templates can serve to analyze PAH emission in a wide variety of objects observed with MIRI-MRS.

2610.19926.abstract: JWST has revealed a population of "dormant'' galaxies at z>3 with strong Balmer breaks and weak emission lines, whose star formation appears to have declined only recently. Whether these galaxies are undergoing a lasting transition toward quiescence or merely experiencing a temporary suppression of star formation remains unclear. We investigate their molecular gas content using archival ALMA observations of [CII]158um and CO rotational transitions. Starting from all publicly available JWST/NIRSpec prism observations and using joint spectrophotometric fitting, we construct a parent sample at z>3 and log(Mstar/Msun)>9.5 in the ALMA-accessible COSMOS, UDS, and GOODS-South fields. Our final sample comprises 7 dormant galaxies and 15 quiescent galaxies with ALMA constraints on their molecular gas content (mostly 3 sigma upper limits). We find that dormant galaxies exhibit systematically lower star formation rates averaged over the past 10Myr (SFR10Myr) than over the past 100Myr (SFR100Myr), supporting a recent rapid decline in their star formation. For the ~70% of the sample with sufficiently constraining ALMA observations, their molecular gas fractions lie at least ~0.3-2dex below those expected for main-sequence galaxies. Moreover, the molecular gas fractions of dormant galaxies show no systematic difference from those of quiescent galaxies in our sample. This indicates that dormant galaxies have already reached a gas-poor state shortly after quenching and favors a scenario in which the rapid shutdown of star formation is associated with depletion or removal of the molecular gas reservoir, rather than primarily with suppressed star formation efficiency while retaining a substantial molecular gas reservoir. Our results suggest that, if no substantial gas replenishment occurs in the future, dormant galaxies are more consistent with becoming "dead'' than with being temporarily "sleeping''.

2610.19937.abstract: JWST observations of massive quiescent galaxies (MQGs) at $z\sim2$ have revealed diverse star formation histories (SFHs). In this letter, we investigate whether these variations are linked to the environment in which MQGs reside, as quantified by the host dark matter halo mass. We identify 12 MQGs from a representative sample of galaxies at $1.6<z<3.5$ obtained by the Blue Jay survey, a JWST Cycle 1 program, and infer their SFHs via modelling of the deep NIRSpec medium-resolution spectra along with multi-band photometry. By correlating the formation and quenching epochs of individual MQGs with their respective host halo masses from the 3D-HST survey, we find that after accounting for the redshift range of the sample ($1.8<z<2.5$), MQGs in more massive haloes formed at significantly earlier cosmic epochs. Meanwhile, although these galaxies also quenched earlier overall, the scatter in quenching epochs across similar halo masses indicates that the quenching process likely involves other contributing factors and is not solely determined by halo mass.

2610.19939.abstract: We present a detailed study of the physical and chemical structure of TMC-1 from the observed spatial distribution of HC3N, NNH+, CN, and their isotopologues, the O-bearing species C18O, C17O, CH3OH, CH3CHO, and H2CO, and the S-bearing species CS, HCS+, H2CS, and H2CCS. The well known filamentary structure of TMC-1 can be interpreted as a single cloud with a velocity gradient perpendicular to the filament, or less likely as due to the alignment of three independent clouds in the line sight with velocities of 5.3-5.7, 5.7-5.9, and 5.9-6.3 km/s. The main contribution to the emission of all studied C-bearing species is found at 5.83 kms/s. We conclude that the three velocity components are dynamically connected and that C-bearing molecules show a different behavior of their abundances compared to O-bearing species, which have emission peaks at 5.7 and 6.25 km/s, and appear at different spatial locations than cyanopolyynes and CnH and CnN radicals. The detection of 13C18O, with exactly the same line profile than that of C18O and C17O, excludes the possibility that the decrease of their emission at 5.83 km/s, could be due to self absorption or absorption by a foreground cloud component. Hence, as indicated by the spatial distribution of C18O and C17O, CO is significantly depleted at the velocities and positions where the emission of the carbon chains and radicals is found. This suggests that the emission of O-bearing species is coming from the external layers of the carbon-rich filaments. A comparison between S-bearing species and other molecules indicates that CS, CCS, HCS+, and H2CS are significantly depleted in the zone of CO depletion. A clear increase of the deuteration of several molecular species is found in the zones where CO and CS are depleted.

2610.19952.abstract: Compactness is widely used to identify candidate relic galaxies, the largely untouched survivors of the first compact massive galaxies. Yet relicness is an evolutionary rather than structural property. Using the COLIBRE cosmological hydrodynamical simulations, we test whether present-day structure traces galaxy formation and assembly histories. Six complementary tracers (stellar age, metallicity, [Mg/Fe], sSFR, velocity dispersion and ex-situ mass fraction) vary coherently across the stellar mass-size plane and independently identify a characteristic compactness scale of $\log_{10}(\Sigma_{1.5,\mathrm{crit}}/(\mathrm{M}_\odot\mathrm{kpc}^{-1.5}))=9.75\pm0.10$. We term this mapping between present-day structure and assembly history morpholography. Combining this threshold with the Degree of Relicness ($\mathrm{DoR}>0.6$), which quantifies early and rapid star formation, we distinguish compact from ancient galaxies and identify 267 relic candidates at their intersection. Ancient galaxies span nearly the full ex-situ-fraction range, from predominantly in-situ formation to substantial merger-driven growth. Relic candidates are concentrated at stellar masses of $\approx 10^{10}$-$10^{11}$ solar masses, host black holes that lie $\approx 0.25$-$2.5$ dex above the median black-hole-stellar-mass relation, and are predominantly satellites (76%), preferentially in cluster environments. Only $\approx 3$% show evidence of strong tidal stripping, suggesting that environment primarily preserves rather than creates relic-like systems. Approximately one third (87/267) are direct descendants of the $z=2$ massive quiescent galaxies identified in COLIBRE. Present-day structure thus retains a statistical fossil record of assembly history, supporting morpholography as a link between nearby galaxies and the early Universe.

2610.20119.title: Uncovering the origin of complex velocity distributions in edge-on disc galaxies

figures.caption: Figure 1: Mock $g$-band image of Galaxy 102 viewed face-on (see Martig et al., 2012). The galaxy has a strong spiral structure that is excited by the satellite seen on the right of the image.

2610.20119.abstract: Stellar line-of-sight velocity distributions are a powerful tool for studying galaxy kinematics and formation history, with multiple-peaked LOSVDs often indicating the presence of complex kinematic components. We extract stellar LOSVDs across the disc of a simulated spiral galaxy viewed edge-on, and study how often and why we see multiple-peaked LOSVDs. We find that the multiple-peaked LOSVDs are mainly found close to the midplane because they result from the presence of spiral arms. This is not because the spiral arms have significantly different kinematics to the disc, but because they correspond to over-densities. Variations in the number of arms present along a line-of-sight create variations in the number of peaks in LOSVDs. This can be used to quantify the strength of the spiral arms above the midplane, and how the thickness of spiral arms vary across the disc. We find that the commonly used fourth order Gauss-Hermite moment, $h_4$, is negative in the regions where there are multiple-peaked LOSVDs, and hence traces spiral arms. Finally, we discuss the observability of the multiple-peaked regions and their associated $h_4$ measurements with current integral field spectrographs. We find that the spectral resolution of MUSE might not be high enough to uncover multiple peaks in LOSVDs when they result from spiral arms, but should allow for identification of the regions of negative $h_4$. On the other hand, higher resolution spectrographs like KOALA and WEAVE may be able to recover multiple peaks in LOSVDs, representing a promising avenue for characterising spiral arms in edge-on disc galaxies.

2610.20260.abstract: Constraining the size of broad-line region (BLR) close to the accretion disk in active galactic nuclei (AGNs) is key to understand the central engine and evolution of AGN. We propose a new method to constrain the BLR size, based on millimeter to sub-millimeter spectral energy distribution (SED), from which a sub-millimeter excess may be found. Such excess can be used to determine the solid angle of the free-free emission region from BLR, as a region with high electron density and optically thick at sub-millimeter wavelength for free-free continuum. Millimeter to sub-millimeter SED analysis toward the central source S1 in a nearby type II AGN NGC 1068 was done, which gave an upper limit on the solid angle of BLR region as(4.94 +/- 0.61) *10^-6 arcsec^2, corresponding to a radius no more than 0.085 pc. Such a constraint on the BLR size is important for estimating the masses of central supermassive black holes in AGNs.

2610.20287.abstract: Galaxy interactions are ubiquitous in the Universe and represent a primary pathway for galaxy growth. Close passages of dwarf galaxies can induce large-scale vertical oscillations in stellar disks, a phenomenon first identified in the Milky Way within the past decade. Here, we use recent red clump distance maps of the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) to show that its stellar periphery is vertically offset from the central disk plane by $\sim$1.2 kpc at radii of $\sim$8.5 kpc and exhibits an S-shaped warp reaching $\sim$3.6 kpc at $\sim$11.5 kpc. We compare these observations to an $N$-body simulation of the LMC-Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) system, in which a direct collision between the Clouds excites vertical oscillations in the outer LMC disk with amplitudes of $\sim$1~kpc and a period of $\sim$600~Myr. The simulated disk best matches the observed vertical structure $\sim$260~Myr after the collision, although this timing depends on the adopted LMC model. At that time, the simulation reproduces the sign and radial onset of the observed offset and the orientation of the warp, but underpredicts the amplitude of the warp by a factor of $\sim$4-5. These results support a collision-driven origin for the large-scale vertical structure of the LMC disk and demonstrate that dwarf--dwarf interactions can reshape stellar disks on galactic scales.

2610.20332.abstract: We present an analysis of 23 Spitzer/IRAC excess galaxies at $5.66 < z < 7.64$, observed as part of the NIRSpec Wide GTO survey. With NIRSpec PRISM spectroscopy, we measure a median rest-frame [OIII]$+\rm{H}\beta$ EW $=1583$~Å, consistent with predictions from the pre-JWST selection and we identify $17/23$ $(\sim74\%)$ of our sample as extreme emission line galaxies (EELGs), based on a selection of [OIII]$+\rm{H}\beta$ EW $\geq1000$~Å. The typical EELG is powered by star-formation rather than active galactic nuclei (AGN) based on their line widths, line ratios and absence of high-ionization lines, though we cannot exclude an AGN contribution in a few individual sources. We find that our luminous ($\langle M_\mathrm{UV}\rangle=-20.7$) EELG sample is characterised by sub-solar metallicities $(7.38 < \rm 12 + \log(O/H) < 8.12)$, young stellar populations ($t_\star \sim 20$ Myr), and enhanced ionizing photon production efficiencies, with median $\log_{10}(\xi_\mathrm{ion}/\mathrm{erg}^{-1}~\mathrm{Hz}) = 25.62$. We find that more UV luminous ($\sim L_\mathrm{UV, z=7}^\ast$) EELGs exhibit systematically lower O32 ratios than fainter ($\sim 0.1\times L_\mathrm{UV}^\ast$) EELGs at fixed [OIII]$+\rm{H}\beta$ EW, indicating less extreme radiation fields and/or lower gas densities than their fainter counterparts. Furthermore, bright EELGs exhibit low neutral hydrogen column densities, consistent with a scenario in which they have largely ionized their circumgalactic medium (CGM). Despite this, we find very low Lyman-$\alpha$ escape fractions ($<2$\%), suggesting these systems reside in relatively small ($\lesssim 0.25$~pMpc) ionized regions of the intergalactic medium (IGM), possibly suggesting that bright galaxies have a minor contribution to reionization.

2610.20475.abstract: The probability of interstellar contact depends not only on the abundance of technological civilizations but also on their spatial connectivity. Treating civilizations as nodes linked whenever their separation is smaller than the distance a signal travels within a communicative lifetime, we determine the radial structure of Galactic civilization networks. An exponential stellar disc replaces the uniform disc of earlier work, and the fraction of stars hosting civilizations may vary with radius as a Galactic Habitable Zone (GHZ). The isolation, contact and network transitions are frontiers several kiloparsecs wide, not boundaries: the contact frontier is set entirely by the disc scale length, and the network frontier, broadened by gradient percolation, stays near 1.5 scale lengths. The two frontiers overlap over a band containing the Sun, where both transitions proceed at once. Within this factorized GHZ model, the radius of peak civilization density depends only logarithmically on the strength of supernova sterilization, and the wide range of published peak radii, from the Galactic centre to 12 kpc, is reproduced primarily by varying that one parameter. Under the present normalization, the location of the zone has only a modest effect on the local contact probability, whereas the modelled Galactic connectivity is minimized when the civilization-density peak lies near the solar Galactocentric radius, where current determinations place the peak.

2610.20505.title: A Step-Like Transition Underlying the Life and Death of Galaxies

The quenched fraction also varies with halo mass, with the trends shown separately for the three $\Sigma_{*}$ regimes. The difference increases continuously with increasing black hole-to-stellar mass ratio. (d) Same as panel (c), but as a function of dark matter halo mass. The difference between the high- and low-$\Sigma_{*}$ quenched fractions shows a weak decreasing trend with increasing halo mass.

Figure 4: An observationally motivated picture for galaxy quenching. At low and intermediate $\Sigma_{*}$, star formation is spatially extended and gas supply is primarily regulated by cooling from the hot circumgalactic halo, making the supply timescale nearly independent of $\Sigma_{*}$. At high $\Sigma_{*}$, star formation and cold gas become increasingly concentrated toward the central region, causing the supply timescale to decrease rapidly. Together with the declining depletion timescale, this naturally makes the two timescales most comparable at intermediate $\Sigma_{*}$ (critical state marked by gray shading), where quenching is most sensitive to changes in the supply timescale. Because SMBH feedback acts most efficiently on centrally concentrated gas, SMBH preferentially increases the supply timescale of high-$\Sigma_{*}$ galaxies, whereas dark matter halos exert a relatively stronger influence on low-$\Sigma_{*}$ galaxies.

(a–c) Quenched fraction as a function of stellar surface density for galaxies divided into three bins of black hole-to-stellar mass ratio ($M_{\rm BH}/M_{*}$). (d–f) Corresponding results for three bins of dark matter halo mass. The overall trends are qualitatively consistent with those found for central galaxies: increasing black hole mass and halo mass both shift the supply-timescale distribution toward longer supply times. Black hole growth also produces a narrower supply-timescale distribution, whereas the width of the distribution shows little dependence on halo mass for satellite galaxies.

Same as Fig. 2(a–c), but using morphology-dependent black hole mass estimates instead of the unified scaling relation [15]. Galaxies are divided into three bins according to their black hole-to-stellar mass ratios ($M_{\rm BH}/M_{*}$). Same as Fig. A3, using morphology-dependent black hole mass estimates instead of the unified scaling relation [15]. Galaxies are divided into three bins according to their black hole-to-stellar mass ratios ($M_{\rm BH}/M_{*}$) derived from the morphology-dependent black hole mass estimators. The inferred supply-timescale distributions show the same dependence on black hole mass as obtained with the unified black hole mass estimator: larger black hole masses shift the supply-timescale distribution toward longer supply times and produce narrower distributions. These results demonstrate that the dependence of the inferred supply-timescale distribution on black hole growth is robust against the adopted black hole mass estimator for both central and satellite galaxies.

(a) Quenched fraction as a function of black hole-to-stellar mass ratio ($M_{\rm BH}/M_{*}$) for galaxies in three stellar surface density regimes. (c) Difference between the quenched fractions at high and low $\Sigma_{*}$, $\Delta F=F_{\rm high\Sigma_{*}}-F_{\rm low\Sigma_{*}}$, as a function of $M_{\rm BH}/M_{*}$. The main difference is that the dependence on halo mass is reversed: in satellite galaxies, halo mass has a stronger influence on the quenched fraction of high-$\Sigma_{*}$ galaxies than on that of low-$\Sigma_{*}$ galaxies.

2610.20505.abstract: How galaxies stop forming stars is a complex and central problem in astrophysics. Numerous physical mechanisms have been proposed, yet a simple, unified framework connecting these mechanisms remains lacking. Here, we derive a step-function quenching response from the fundamental principle of gas mass conservation, governed by the competition between gas-supply and gas-depletion timescales. This response also enables the gas-supply timescale to be inferred from the observed quenched fraction. Applying this method to approximately 350,000 galaxies, we find a characteristic gas-supply timescale of ~1 Gyr, reveal distinct inside-out and outside-in quenching signatures associated with supermassive black holes and dark matter halos, respectively, and identify galaxies with intermediate stellar surface mass densities as occupying a critical state for quenching and rejuvenation. Our work establishes a unified physical framework in which a simple step-function response captures how diverse physical processes regulate galaxy quenching and the resumption of star formation through their effects on the competition between gas-supply and gas-depletion timescales.

2610.20557.abstract: Supermassive black hole binaries (SMBHB) are expected at the center of galaxies as a result of galaxy mergers. The dynamics and evolution of SMBHBs shed light on the evolution and formation of galaxies, the gravitational wave background and the nature of gravity. Many methods have been proposed to identify sub-parsec SMBHBs via the detection of gravitational waves or the modulation of the emission from the surrounding gaseous environment. In a previous study, we proposed a new method of identifying SMBHBs in non-active galactic nuclei via gravitational lensing. The caustics, i.e. the source positions with a divergent magnification, exhibit a complex extended geometry which rotates with the binary period. Each caustic-crossing produces an extreme magnification by up to a factor of $10^{6}$. In this work, we generalize the previous study and describe the rich phenomenology of binary-lens amplification of starlight (BLAST). We explore the electromagnetic transients produced when accounting for the relative proper motion of the source, either a single or a binary star, the eccentricity and precession of the SMBHB, and the relative inclination. Systems where a star rapidly drifts across the caustic produce a single- or double-peaked flare. In the opposite limit, a star with no relative proper motion produces quasi-periodic lensed starlight (QPLS), i.e., repeated peaks that track the system's orbital evolution. We determine the expected magnification and peak duration in different circumstances, and calculate the magnification curves and their Fourier transforms. This study may help construct search pipelines to identify SMBHBs in electromagnetic time-domain surveys.

2610.18957.abstract: Merging galaxy clusters provide an ideal laboratory for testing the self-interacting nature of dark matter. In this paper, we present a pilot study of magnetohydrodynamical cosmological zoom-in simulations of two cluster mergers selected from TNG-Cluster, with $M_{\rm 200c} \sim 9\times10^{14}~M_\odot$ and $M_{\rm 200c}\sim 2\times10^{14}~M_\odot$. The simulations are performed with both standard collisionless cold dark matter (CDM) and self-interacting dark matter (SIDM), assuming an isotropic, velocity-independent cross-section of $\sigma_{\rm T}/m_\chi = 1~\rm cm^2~g^{-1}$, with an additional $0.5~\rm cm^2~g^{-1}$ run for the low-mass system, and the mass resolution and galaxy formation model are unchanged from TNG-Cluster. We show how dark matter self-interactions produce an isothermal core in the dark matter halo, generate unique substructures in the intracluster light, and introduce variation in the multi-wavelength observables of the intracluster plasma. Using these simulations, we test the validity of observational probes for dark matter self-interactions in cluster mergers. We find that the shock-to-shock separation shows similar evolution in the self-interaction models tested here, providing a reference for distinguishing the $\sim100-200~\rm kpc$-scale difference in halo separation induced by self-interactions. Moreover, the dark matter halo centroid of the main cluster in the massive cluster merger is offset from the brightest cluster galaxy by as much as $\sim20~\rm kpc$, larger than the offset in the sub-cluster. This offset persists beyond 4 Gyr after the first pericenter passage. Our results indicate that sample selection plays a key role in testing the possible self-interacting nature of dark matter using cluster mergers, and that double radio relic cluster mergers and massive clusters with evidence of an ancient major merger offer a promising testbed for this purpose.

2610.18995.abstract: We present the first results of a series of studies based on JWST observations of the globular cluster 47 Tucanae (47 Tuc, or NGC 104) obtained with NIRCam. By combining new data with earlier JWST observations, we derive high-precision proper motions (PMs) over a multi-year baseline (of ~3 years) and construct a clean sample of cluster members extending to very faint magnitudes (F444W~24.25 mag, corresponding to ~0.077 solar masses, slightly above the estimated hydrogen-burning limit of 47 Tuc, ~0.074 solar masses) along the main sequence (MS). We investigated the presence of the low-mass MS kink previously identified in 47 Tuc using the new F090W and F444W photometry. No significant signature of the feature is found using these filters, consistent with its proposed physical interpretation as a consequence of the transition in carbon chemistry toward a methane-dominated equilibrium in very low-mass stars. A comparison with theoretical isochrones indicates that the stellar population near the bottom of the MS is likely dominated by oxygen-poor stars, in agreement with previous findings. Using artificial-star tests, we quantify the completeness of our sample and show that the requirement of PM-based membership significantly limits the detection of the faintest objects, indicating that current JWST observations of 47 Tuc are not sufficiently deep to reliably trace the cluster's brown dwarf cooling sequence. The mass function (MF) of 47 Tuc shows a structured behaviour, with a break at ~0.15 solar masses not associated with the onset of convection, and a mild but systematic radial variation consistent with mass segregation. Our analysis indicates that the MF shape in this mass regime is more complex than a simple power-law description. This feature in the MF may point to a presently unrecognised mechanism affecting the formation or dynamical evolution of low-mass stars in globular clusters.

2610.18996.abstract: We used a combination of James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and Hubble Space Telescope (HST) observations to investigate the mass functions (MFs) of the different stellar populations in the globular cluster (GC) 47 Tucanae (NGC 104) over a wide stellar-mass interval. We identified the multiple populations along the lower main sequence using only JWST photometry and, in particular, colour combinations sensitive to variations in oxygen abundance. We derived the MFs of the first- and second-population (1P and 2P) stars separately and found that in the low-mass regime, the present-day MF of the 1P population is significantly steeper than that of the 2P population, which appears nearly flat. We also present the results of a dynamical model showing that this behaviour requires a different initial mass function (IMF) for the 2P and the 1P populations in the 0.1-0.4 solar masses mass range, thus providing a new fundamental constraint for the study of the star formation of multiple populations in GCs.

2610.19244.abstract: We present a systematic spectroscopic study of hydrogen Brackett-alpha (Br-alpha) and carbon monoxide (CO) fundamental-band (4.3-5.2 micron) emission from a homogeneous sample of 0.2-1.5 Msun pre-main-sequence (PMS) stars in the Orion Nebula observed with JWST/NIRSpec-MOS as part of our Chandra-JWST project. Using 73 Br-alpha and 46 CO spectra, we investigate correlations between warm-gas emission, stellar properties, accretion, and environment with censored correlation and regression analyses accounting for multiple testing. Br-alpha luminosity correlates strongly with accretion luminosity (Lacc), even after excluding sources within 2' of Theta1 Ori C, the nebula's main ionizing O-type star, whose radiation may bias proplyd Lacc estimates. This supports Br-alpha as a robust empirical tracer of accretion in PMS stars. Br-alpha also correlates with visual extinction (Av) and more weakly with stellar bolometric luminosity and mass. CO fundamental-band luminosities likewise correlate positively with Lacc and Av, relationships that persist in a larger combined JWST/NIRSpec+MIRI sample spanning multiple star-forming regions. In contrast to Br-alpha, CO luminosity shows no significant dependence on basic stellar properties, suggesting that warm molecular gas is governed primarily by accretion and local disk conditions. The weaker correlations of the Spitzer/IRAC spectral slope with Lacc and Av suggest that warm inner-disk gas may evolve or disperse faster than optically thick dust. Overall, the CO results tentatively indicate declining warm-gas emission as disks evolve, modulated by accretion-powered thermal and ultraviolet excitation, although variations in emitting area inherited from natal core conditions may also contribute.

2610.19297.abstract: Using three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulations accounting for ohmic dissipation, we investigate the long-term evolution of the infalling envelope for $\sim 100,000$\,yr after protostar formation. The primary control parameter is the initial misalignment angle $\theta_0$ between the rotation axis and the magnetic field, varied from $0^\circ$ to $90^\circ$. In all misaligned models ($\theta_0 e 0^\circ$), the pseudodisk (or infalling envelope) surrounding the circumstellar disk develops a highly distorted and complex morphology. Gas accretion from the envelope proceeds through discrete, channel-like flows, producing asymmetric streams rather than axisymmetric infall. Protostellar outflows are launched even in these complex environments, and inflow and outflow regions are strongly interwoven. Outflows transport angular momentum anisotropically, leading to time-dependent changes in disk orientation and outflow direction, which further enhance envelope asymmetry. We examine the relative orientation between gas flows and magnetic fields and find that, although statistical tendencies exist, accretion streams cannot be uniquely characterized as either parallel or perpendicular to the magnetic field, particularly in strongly misaligned cases. We also show that most infalling gas accretes at nearly the free-fall velocity, with only a minor fraction significantly slowed within the pseudodisk. Asymmetric accretion and stream-like structures persist beyond 10,000\,au, demonstrating that large-scale asymmetry can arise intrinsically. Our results show that complex streams and asymmetric envelopes naturally emerge from magnetized core physics, even in the absence of initial turbulence or external gas accretion.

2610.19313.abstract: Ultraviolet (UV) observations offer unique insights into transient and variable astrophysical phenomena, from the Sun and nearby stars to supernovae and star-forming galaxies. Here, we summarise and review the diagnostic power of the UV spectrum for probing the physical conditions, dynamics and energetics of these events. We trace the historical development of UV astronomy from early satellite missions to the current landscape shaped by the Hubble Space Telescope, the GALaxy Evolution eXplorer, the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory and AstroSat/UVIT. Particular emphasis is placed on resonance lines such as Mg II $h$ and $k$, C II, Si IV, C IV and N V, which probe the (solar and) stellar chromosphere and transition region, revealing magnetic heating, shocks and mass loss across stellar types. We examine UV diagnostics of stellar flares, pre-main-sequence activity and rotation--activity correlations, linking them to exoplanetary irradiation and habitability. We then explore the UV view of supernova shock breakout and early-time emission, as well as the far-UV mapping of young stellar populations and hierarchical star formation in the Magellanic Clouds. Together, these aspects illustrate how the UV connects small-scale plasma processes to galactic-scale star formation. Despite remarkable progress, UV transient astronomy remains limited by instrument availability and cadence. Forthcoming missions promise to transform this field by capturing the rapid, luminous phenomena that define the dynamic Universe.

2610.19879.abstract: Galactic nuclei, with the central supermassive black holes (SMBHs) and surrounding dense star clusters, serve as natural laboratories for studying gravitational dynamics in extreme gravitational environments. In this work, we model the long term evolution of black hole binaries (BHBs) in these environments by incorporating the tidal influence of the central SMBH, the potential of the nuclear star cluster, SMBH induced relativistic precession, and stochastic perturbations from stellar flybys. Our numerical simulations show that the long term evolution of BHBs is predominantly governed by the SMBH-driven ZLK mechanism. However, once stellar flybys are included, they can modify both the binary angular momentum and energy. The cumulative effect of repeated flyby encounters substantially reshapes the long term dynamical evolution, eventually leading systems toward either merger or disruption. Based on a population synthesis study, we find that this combined secular and non-secular channel produces a merger rate of approximately $\mathcal{R}\simeq16\mathrm{Gpc^{-3}yr^{-1}}$, which is significantly higher than the rates predicted by dynamical channels that neglect stellar flybys. Furthermore, we predict that a non-negligible fraction of merging systems would retain detectable eccentricities at low frequencies around 5 Hz, thus providing a distinctive observational signature for next generation ground based GW detectors. Our results demonstrate that the stochastic perturbations from the surrounding environment are essential for modeling BHB evolution in galactic nuclei, and that this channel may contribute a major fraction of observed mergers.

2610.19989.abstract: Classical novae eject material during thermonuclear eruptions on accreting white dwarfs, forming expanding shells whose structures and kinematics provide insights into the eruption mechanism and binary interaction. However, their intrinsic three-dimensional (3D) structures remain poorly constrained. We present the first 3D catalog of nova shells based on integral field spectroscopy, enabling us to investigate their structures beyond projection effects. We compiled observations of 19 nova shells obtained with MUSE at the VLT, complemented by new MEGARA observations at the GTC and WEAVE observations at the WHT. We constructed 3D visualizations of selected emission lines to explore the diversity of shell morphologies and kinematics. The shells reveal a wide variety of structures, including ellipsoidal or spherical shells, rings, bipolar features, and clumpy or irregular components, many of which are not apparent in 2D projections. Approximately 60% of the sample exhibits predominantly ellipsoidal or spherical shapes, while about 30% shows ring-like or bipolar structures. Several objects display strong line-dependent morphological differences, with [O III] or [N II] tracing distinct kinematic components from those seen in H${\alpha}$. Compared with imaging studies, integral field spectroscopy reveals a larger fraction of bipolar or toroidal shells. The differences between emission lines highlight the diverse excitation mechanisms and physical conditions within the ejecta. Finally, comparing expansion velocities in the plane of the sky and along the line of sight suggests low intrinsic aspect ratios, consistent with estimates from projected shell shapes.

2610.20495.abstract: A subset of active galactic nuclei (AGN) manifests as compact radio sources with peaked radio spectra, commonly referred to as peaked-spectrum (PS) sources. Generally, PS sources are interpreted as young radio jets, but the early evolution of the jet is rarely observed and not fully understood. Here, we present VT J182357-234511 (VT J1823-2345), a radio transient in the Very Large Array Sky Survey (VLASS) that resembles a PS source. Notable properties of VT J1823-2345 include: (i) brightening by a factor of 3 between 1996 and 2021 at 1.4 GHz, (ii) peaked spectra with high frequency peaks at $u_{\mathrm{p,obs}}\gtrsim6\,\mathrm{GHz}$, (iii) a peaked 3 GHz light curve that has been fading since 2023, (iv) a resolved Gaussian (major-axis) size of 0.4 mas in 2024, and (v) a linear polarization fraction $p_{\mathrm{L}}\simeq0.73\%$ at 8.8 GHz with an extreme Faraday rotation measure $\mathrm{RM_{\mathrm{obs}}} \sim +12,000\,\mathrm{rad}\,\mathrm{m}^{-2}$. On the sky, VT J1823-2345 coincides with a supernova remnant and an F-type star, but no background galaxy is seen. Based on the multi-wavelength properties, we disfavor Galactic transients, explosive extragalactic transients, and blazar variability as plausible explanations. We argue that VT J1823-2345 is consistent with a "short-lived" parsec-scale PS source with a decades-old jet that does not grow into a large-scale radio galaxy. From comparing the full VLASS light curves, we speculate that VT J1823-2345 is similar to many VLASS nuclear transients reported in the literature, which may represent an emerging class of transient radio jets, perhaps related to episodic AGN activity or jetted tidal disruption events.

2610.20507.abstract: No: neither through the bosenovae of gravitational atoms formed around stars and compact objects, nor through those of boson stars formed in the galactic dark-matter halo. We assume that all the dark matter consists of ultralight bosons with attractive self-interactions, which can be captured in the gravitational potential of astrophysical objects or condense into self-gravitating configurations. When these systems collapse in a bosenova, part of their mass is turned into relativistic radiation that escapes the galaxy. We bound the mass that a single object can eject and sum it over realistic models of the Milky Way and of other types of galaxies. For gravitational atoms, with realistic stellar populations and stellar evolution, the stars of the Milky Way deplete at most $\epsilon^{\rm GA}_\star\simeq3\times10^{-9}$ of its halo, and the pump is equally negligible in other galaxies. The central black hole, Sgr A$^*$, could reach $\epsilon^{\rm GA}\sim10^{-3}$, but only for a boson mass disfavoured by ultrafaint dwarf galaxies and beyond the validity of the perturbative treatment, where only a geometric bound on the dark matter flux is available. For boson stars feeding on the rest of the halo, these would radiate at most $\sim3\times10^{-5}$ of the Milky-Way halo and $0.1\%$ of a DF2-like one.
